slides.title: The Key Distribution Problem
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Diffie & Hellman (1976), IEEE Transactions on Information Theory. GCHQ's James Ellis and Clifford Cocks had a classified equivalent earlier, declassified 1997.

Misconception: Students think asymmetric crypto 'replaced' symmetric crypto. It solved a different problem (key distribution), not raw encryption speed.

Analogy: Before 1976, secure communication required a shared secret handshake agreed in person. Diffie-Hellman is like inventing a way for two strangers to agree on a handshake by shouting across a crowded room without anyone else being able to reproduce it.

Exam tip: Be ready to name the key distribution problem as the motivating flaw asymmetric cryptography was invented to solve.
bullets: Symmetric cryptography: same key locks and unlocks, fast, but requires a pre-shared secret
The chicken-and-egg problem: how do two strangers agree on a secret key without an already-secure channel?
1976 breakthrough: Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman publish 'New Directions in Cryptography'
The proposal: a cipher where the encryption key and decryption key are mathematically related but computationally distinct
Why it matters: solves key distribution with math instead of couriers, diplomatic pouches, or codebooks

content_blocks: Every symmetric cipher shares one unavoidable flaw: both parties need the same secret key before they can communicate securely, but transmitting that key itself requires a secure channel they don't yet have. This is the key distribution problem, and for most of cryptographic history it had no elegant solution, only logistics like trusted couriers.

In 1976, Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published a paper proposing something radically different: a cipher built from two mathematically linked keys, one that can be shared openly and one that must stay secret, such that knowing the public one does not reveal the private one in any practical amount of time.

slides.title: Public and Private Keys: The Padlock Model
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 governs key-management lifecycle requirements for asymmetric keys, including generation, storage, and rotation.

Misconception: Students think 'encrypting with a private key' is literally the same operation as normal encryption. It is a distinct signing operation applied to a hash, covered later in this section.

Analogy (Professor's Note, the padlock): The public key is an open padlock you hand out freely; the private key is the one physical key that opens it. Anyone can snap the padlock shut (encrypt); only you can open it (decrypt). Flip it for signatures: you stamp a wax seal with your private key that only your public 'seal pattern' can confirm came from your ring.

Exam tip: Match 'encrypt with public key' to confidentiality and 'sign with private key' to authentication/non-repudiation, this pairing is tested directly.
bullets: Key pair: each participant generates a mathematically linked public key and private key together
Public key: freely distributed, published in a certificate, keyserver, or browser trust store
Private key: never leaves its owner's control; compromise breaks every guarantee the system provides
Confidentiality path: encrypt with recipient's public key -> only their private key can decrypt
Authentication path: 'encrypt' with your own private key -> anyone with your public key can verify it came from you

content_blocks: Asymmetric cryptography (also called public-key cryptography) gives each participant a key pair: a public key that can be freely distributed, and a private key that never leaves its owner's control. The two directions of use are complementary. If a sender encrypts with the recipient's public key, only the holder of the matching private key can decrypt it, providing confidentiality. If a sender instead performs the operation with their own private key, anyone holding the matching public key can verify the operation could only have come from that private key's owner, providing authentication and non-repudiation via digital signatures.

slides.title: Trapdoor Functions: Easy Forward, Hard in Reverse
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Formalized by Diffie & Hellman (1976); RSA (1977) was the first practical realized trapdoor function used for both encryption and signatures. ECC is standardized in FIPS 186-5 and SEC 2.

Misconception: Students think RSA is 'unbreakable'. It is computationally infeasible with current classical hardware for sufficiently large keys, not mathematically impossible. Shor's algorithm threatens it on a sufficiently large quantum computer, motivating NIST post-quantum standards (FIPS 203/204/205).

Analogy: Mixing paint colors together is trivial; un-mixing them back into the exact original colors is essentially impossible. That one-way mixing is the trapdoor.

Exam tip: Know that RSA's trapdoor is factoring; ECC's trapdoor is the discrete logarithm problem, these are two different math problems, not the same one applied twice.
bullets: Trapdoor function: easy to compute forward, infeasible to reverse without a secret 'trapdoor'
RSA's trapdoor: multiplying two huge primes is trivial; factoring the product back apart is not
Integer factorization problem: no known efficient classical algorithm for large numbers
ECC's trapdoor: the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem, different math, same asymmetry idea
Security rests on math, not secrecy: the algorithms are public; only the private key is secret

content_blocks: The security of asymmetric schemes does not rest on secrecy of the algorithm itself, it rests on a class of mathematical problems that are easy to compute in one direction but believed computationally infeasible to reverse without extra information, called trapdoor functions. RSA's trapdoor is the integer factorization problem: multiplying two enormous primes is trivial for a computer, but recovering those two original primes from only their product is, for sufficiently large numbers, believed to require more computation than is practical with any near-future classical hardware.

Elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) instead relies on the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem, offering equivalent security with far smaller keys and faster computation, a critical advantage for mobile devices, IoT hardware, and high-throughput TLS termination.

slides.title: The Hybrid Cryptosystem: Why Your Browser Never 'Just Uses RSA'
slides.speaker_notes:
Context (Real-World Context, Why Your Browser Never 'Just Uses RSA'): RSA or ECDHE runs for only a few milliseconds at the very start of a TLS connection, just long enough to authenticate the server and agree on a session key. Every byte of the actual page that follows is encrypted with AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305. TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) explicitly separates the handshake's key-establishment phase from the record layer's bulk encryption phase.

Misconception: 'HTTPS means the whole page is encrypted with RSA.' False, see above.

Analogy: Asymmetric crypto is the armored car that delivers the vault combination once; the symmetric cipher is the vault itself doing the heavy daily lifting.

Exam tip: If asked why TLS doesn't use RSA for the entire session, answer: performance, asymmetric ops are used only to establish a symmetric session key.
bullets: Asymmetric is slow: RSA/ECC operations are orders of magnitude slower than symmetric ciphers like AES
The pattern: use asymmetric crypto sparingly to authenticate and establish a shared symmetric session key
Then switch: all bulk data is encrypted with a fast symmetric cipher using that session key
Nearly universal: TLS, SSH, S/MIME, IPsec are all hybrid cryptosystems
Common misconception: HTTPS is not 'the whole page encrypted with RSA', RSA/ECDHE only runs for milliseconds at connection start

content_blocks: Asymmetric cryptography is not good at raw bulk encryption of large amounts of data, the mathematical operations underlying RSA and ECC are orders of magnitude slower than symmetric ciphers such as AES. In practice, essentially every real-world protocol uses a hybrid cryptosystem: asymmetric operations authenticate participants and establish a shared symmetric session key, after which all bulk traffic is encrypted with a fast symmetric cipher.

This tradeoff, using the mathematically elegant but computationally expensive asymmetric primitives only where their unique properties (no pre-shared secret, verifiable identity) are actually needed, is one of the most important architectural lessons in applied cryptography.

slides.title: RSA Key Generation: The Arithmetic Skeleton
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Modern deployments use n values of 2048 or 4096 bits. Primality is confirmed with probabilistic tests such as Miller-Rabin.

Misconception: Students think e and d are chosen independently. d is mathematically derived from e and φ(n), they are inseparably linked.

Analogy: p and q are the two secret ingredients of a recipe; n is the finished dish anyone can taste (see publicly) but can't easily reverse-engineer back into the exact original ingredients.

Exam tip: Know the roles: p, q (secret primes) -> n (public modulus) -> e (public exponent) -> d (private exponent, derived, secret).
bullets: Step 1: select two large random primes, p and q
Step 2: compute the modulus n = p × q, published as part of the public key
Step 3: choose a public exponent e (commonly 65537) and compute private exponent d
d is the modular multiplicative inverse of e with respect to φ(n), Euler's totient of n
Result: public key = (e, n); private key = (d, n), factoring n back to p and q is what breaks the scheme

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Modern deployments use n values of 2048 or 4096 bits. Primality is confirmed with probabilistic tests such as Miller-Rabin.

Misconception: Students think e and d are chosen independently. d is mathematically derived from e and φ(n), they are inseparably linked.

Analogy: p and q are the two secret ingredients of a recipe; n is the finished dish anyone can taste (see publicly) but can't easily reverse-engineer back into the exact original ingredients.

Exam tip: Know the roles: p, q (secret primes) -> n (public modulus) -> e (public exponent) -> d (private exponent, derived, secret).
content_blocks: Key generation begins by selecting two large, random prime numbers, conventionally labeled p and q. Their product n = p × q becomes the modulus published as part of the public key. A public exponent e (commonly 65537, chosen for computational efficiency and resistance to low-exponent attacks) is selected, and a private exponent d is computed such that d is the modular multiplicative inverse of e with respect to φ(n), Euler's totient of n. The public key is the pair (e, n); the private key is the pair (d, n).
Because d can only feasibly be derived from e and n by an attacker who has also factored n back into p and q, the entire scheme's security reduces directly to the difficulty of the factoring problem.

slides.title: Encryption and Decryption via Modular Exponentiation
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: The following commands demonstrate real RSA key generation and inspection with OpenSSL, the same toolkit examined later in the Heartbleed case study.

Misconception: Students think RSA encrypts the message directly with complex logic. It's one operation, modular exponentiation, applied twice (once with e, once with d).

Analogy: Think of a combination lock dial: turning it forward (encrypt) by a known amount is easy; figuring out how far it turned just from the final position (decrypt without the key) is what you can't do without the secret.

Exam tip: Memorize c = m^e mod n and m = c^d mod n cold, this notation appears directly on free-response questions.
bullets: Encryption: c = m^e mod n, using the public key (e, n)
Decryption: m = c^d mod n, using the private key (d, n)
Modular exponentiation is the single arithmetic operation RSA performs for both directions
Forward is fast: square-and-multiply algorithms make this efficient even for huge exponents
Reverse is hard: recovering m from c without d requires factoring n or solving the RSA problem directly

content_blocks: Encryption and decryption both take the form of modular exponentiation: c = m^e mod n to encrypt plaintext m into ciphertext c, and m = c^d mod n to recover it. Efficient algorithms like square-and-multiply make this fast even for enormous exponents, while the inverse operation, without knowing d, remains computationally infeasible.
This is why OpenSSL, the reference cryptography toolkit used throughout the industry, exposes commands to generate an RSA key pair and inspect its components directly.

code_block.content:
# Generate a 2048-bit RSA private key (public key is derivable from it)
openssl genrsa -out server.key 2048

# Inspect the key's mathematical components: modulus, public exponent, private exponent
openssl rsa -in server.key -text -noout | head -n 20

# Extract just the public key half, safe to distribute
openssl rsa -in server.key -pubout -out server_public.pem

slides.title: Digital Signatures: Signing the Hash, Not the Message
slides.speaker_notes:
Context (Critical Concept, Signing Is Not Encrypting): A common student error is describing a digital signature as 'encrypting the message with the private key.' In real implementations, the private key operation is applied to a hash of the message, not the message itself, signing a multi-gigabyte file directly with slow RSA arithmetic would be impractical. Every signing command includes -sha256 for exactly this reason.

Misconception: See above, keep the pipeline straight: hash first, sign the hash, verify by re-hashing and comparing.

Analogy: A notary doesn't retype your entire contract from memory to prove it's authentic, they stamp a unique seal onto a summary (the hash) that anyone can check against the original document.

Exam tip: If asked to explain signatures, always mention the hash step explicitly, omitting it is the most common way to lose credit.
bullets: Sign: hash the message, then encrypt that hash with your own private key
Verify: recompute the hash, decrypt the received signature with the public key, compare
Why hash first: asymmetric operations are slow, hashing compresses arbitrary-length input to a fixed digest
Three guarantees at once: authentication, integrity, and non-repudiation
Critical distinction: signing is NOT 'encrypting the message with the private key'

content_blocks: Digital signatures reverse the roles of encryption: to sign a document, the signer computes a cryptographic hash of the message and encrypts that hash with their own private key, producing the signature. Anyone with the signer's public key can independently hash the same message, decrypt the received signature using the public key, and confirm the two hashes match.

Because computing the correct signature requires the private key, and because the hash guarantees any alteration to the message would produce a completely different digest, this mechanism simultaneously provides authentication, integrity, and non-repudiation.

# Sign a file: hash it with SHA-256, then encrypt the digest with the private key
openssl dgst -sha256 -sign server.key -out contract.sig contract.pdf

# Verify the signature using only the public key -- no secret needed to verify
openssl dgst -sha256 -verify server_public.pem -signature contract.sig contract.pdf
# Output: "Verified OK" if, and only if, the file is byte-identical to what was signed

slides.title: Public Key Infrastructure: Binding Identity to Keys
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: RFC 5280 defines the X.509 certificate format. Examples of CAs include DigiCert, Let's Encrypt, Sectigo, governed by CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements.

Misconception: Students think a certificate 'is' encryption. It's an identity binding, the certificate just carries a public key plus a trusted signature vouching for who owns it.

Analogy: A CA is like a notary public or a passport office, it doesn't do your traveling for you, it just vouches that the passport (certificate) really belongs to the person presenting it.

Exam tip: Root CAs keep private keys offline and use intermediates for day-to-day issuance, know this limits blast radius if an intermediate is compromised.

Certificate Authority (CA): a trusted third party that verifies identity and signs a certificate binding it to a public key
X.509 certificate: bundles a public key with identity info and the issuing CA's signature
Chain of trust: root CA signs intermediate, intermediate signs end-entity certificate
Root of trust: root certificates are self-signed, trusted only because OS/browser vendors pre-install them after audits

slides.speaker_notes:

content_blocks: Distributing raw public keys with no attached proof of identity solves the mathematics but not the trust problem: anyone can generate a key pair and claim to be 'your bank.' Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) solves this by introducing Certificate Authorities (CAs), which cryptographically vouch for the binding between an identity and a public key by issuing an X.509 certificate.

Because a CA's signature on a certificate is itself just another asymmetric-signature operation, trust extends transitively: a root CA signs an intermediate CA's certificate, and that intermediate signs the end-entity certificate, forming a chain of trust that can be validated without the relying party ever having met the end-entity in advance. Root certificates are self-signed and trusted only because they are pre-installed by OS and browser vendors after extensive audits.

slides.title: Self-Signed Certificates and the CSR Workflow
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: NIST SP 800-57 and CA/Browser Forum guidelines both treat unvalidated self-signed certificates in production as a critical control gap.

Misconception: 'Self-signed means broken crypto.' No, the math works fine; what's missing is third-party identity verification.

Analogy: A self-signed certificate is like a business card you printed yourself claiming to be a bank president, the card can look perfectly official, but nobody outside verified the claim.

Exam tip: A CN (common name) mismatch or an unexpectedly self-signed cert in production logs is a textbook indicator of misconfiguration or active interception, this exact scenario appears in the practice section later.
bullets: Self-signed certificate: issuer and subject are the same entity, no third party verified it
Mathematically valid, trust-wise empty: structurally identical to a CA-issued cert but carries no identity verification
Real risk: a client that fails to properly validate the chain will accept any self-signed cert, including spoofed names
Legitimate use: internal testing and lab environments
Dangerous use: disabling verification (verify=False, curl -k) in production

# Generate a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) and a self-signed certificate
# for lab/testing purposes, valid for 365 days
openssl req -new -x509 -key server.key -out server.crt -days 365 \

openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -text | grep -A2 "Validity\|Subject:\|Issuer:"

slides.title: The TLS Handshake: PKI and Hybrid Crypto Together
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3) mandates forward-secret key exchange for all cipher suites, removing the legacy static RSA key-transport mode.

Misconception: 'Forward secrecy' sounds abstract, tie it concretely to: even if the server's long-term private key leaks tomorrow, today's captured traffic stays undecryptable because the session key was ephemeral and discarded.

Analogy: Each TLS session gets its own one-time-use combination lock generated fresh; stealing the master key factory blueprint later doesn't reopen locks that were already thrown away.

quiz.question: Roughly which ECDSA key size provides security equivalent to a 2048-bit RSA key, per NIST SP 800-57?
options: ECDSA keys cannot be meaningfully compared to RSA key sizes
quiz.explanation: Option B is correct: NIST SP 800-57 places RSA-2048 at roughly 112-bit symmetric-equivalent security, matched by ECDSA P-256's 256-bit key. Option A (P-521) corresponds to a much higher security level, closer to RSA-15360. Option C is not a standard curve size. Option D is false -- NIST publishes exactly this equivalence table.

slides.title: Case Study: Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160)
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: CVE-2014-0160. Affected OpenSSL versions 1.0.1 through 1.0.1f.

Misconception: 'It's just a memory bug, nothing to do with crypto.' The devastating part is specifically that it leaked the private keys underpinning the asymmetric trust model, not just generic memory.

Analogy: Like a bank vault with a side door that, if you ask politely with the wrong phrasing, hands you a stack of random papers from the vault floor, usually junk, but sometimes the master key.

Exam tip: Connect Heartbleed directly to forward secrecy from Section II: sessions negotiated with forward-secret ECDHE were NOT retroactively decryptable even after key theft; static RSA key-transport sessions were.
bullets: What it was: a buffer over-read in OpenSSL's TLS heartbeat extension, disclosed April 2014
The bug: a missing bounds check let a malformed heartbeat request leak up to 64KB of server memory per request
What leaked: private keys, session cookies, and plaintext credentials sitting in adjacent memory
Scale: affected roughly 17% of the internet's TLS-enabled web servers at disclosure
Worst case: a leaked RSA private key means every past non-forward-secret session becomes decryptable

content_blocks: In April 2014, security researchers publicly disclosed Heartbleed, a flaw in OpenSSL's implementation of the TLS heartbeat extension (RFC 6520), a keepalive mechanism unrelated to core cryptographic operations. The bug was a simple missing bounds check: a client could send a heartbeat request claiming a payload length far larger than the data actually supplied, and the vulnerable server would blindly copy that claimed length of memory back into its response, silently leaking whatever adjacent bytes happened to be in the process's heap, frequently including private keys, session tokens, and plaintext credentials.

Once an attacker holds the private key corresponding to a certificate's public key, every previously captured TLS session using non-forward-secret cipher suites becomes decryptable, and the attacker can impersonate the server indefinitely by presenting the legitimate certificate alongside the stolen key.

slides.title: Heartbleed's Real Lesson: Patching Is Not Enough
slides.speaker_notes:
Context (Critical Concept): Organizations that patched but did not reissue certificates remained exposed to any attacker who had captured a key during the vulnerability window, a mistake documented across thousands of affected domains in 2014.

Misconception: 'Patched = safe again.' A patch closes the hole going forward; it cannot retroactively secure a secret that already left the building.

Analogy: Changing the locks after a burglar copied your house key stops future break-ins through that door, but it doesn't undo the fact that they already photographed everything inside during the burglary.

Exam tip: If a scenario describes a patched vulnerability that previously leaked secrets, always mention credential/key rotation as a required, separate remediation step.
bullets: Two separate remediation steps: patch the software AND rotate/reissue the keys
Why patching alone fails: it stops future leaks but does nothing to un-leak a key already stolen
Required response: revoke and reissue certificates across affected infrastructure
Real-world gap: many organizations patched OpenSSL but never reissued certificates
Broader lesson: incident response for key compromise ≠ incident response for a software bug

slides.title: Case Study: The DigiNotar CA Compromise (2011)
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Estimated 300,000+ Iranian Gmail users affected. DigiNotar was subsequently distrusted by all major browser vendors.

Misconception: 'The math failed.' No, this is the definitive case study of PKI's systemic fragility: trust is only as strong as the least-secure CA anywhere in the global trust store, because any trusted CA can issue a certificate for any domain.

Analogy: It's not that the notary's stamp was forged, the notary's own office was broken into and the real stamp was used to notarize fake documents.

Exam tip: Contrast this with Heartbleed: Heartbleed compromised an end-entity's private key; DigiNotar compromised a CA's private key, which is far more systemically dangerous because a CA can vouch for ANY domain.
bullets: What happened: attackers breached a trusted Dutch CA and issued 500+ fraudulent, validly-signed certificates
Including: a wildcard certificate for *.google.com
Why it passed checks: the fraudulent certs were signed with DigiNotar's legitimate CA key, the crypto itself wasn't broken
Impact: large-scale man-in-the-middle interception of Gmail traffic, notably against users in Iran
Outcome: DigiNotar was distrusted by all major browsers and declared bankrupt within months

content_blocks: In mid-2011, attackers breached DigiNotar, a Dutch Certificate Authority trusted by every major browser and OS at the time. The attackers gained administrative control of DigiNotar's certificate-issuance systems and used that access to issue over 500 fraudulent but perfectly valid certificates for domains they did not own, including a wildcard certificate for *.google.com. Because these certificates were signed with DigiNotar's legitimate CA private key, they passed every technical chain-of-trust check a browser could perform; nothing about the cryptography itself was broken.

The forged certificates were used to conduct large-scale man-in-the-middle interception of Gmail traffic, most notably against users in Iran, who unknowingly connected through attacker-controlled infrastructure presenting a completely valid-looking google.com certificate.

slides.title: The Response: Certificate Transparency and Let's Encrypt
slides.speaker_notes:
Context (Real-World Context, Democratization of PKI): Prior to 2016, obtaining a trusted TLS certificate typically cost money and required manual validation, leaving a large fraction of the web on plaintext HTTP. Misconception: Students treat CT and Let's Encrypt as unrelated. Both are systemic PKI-hardening responses, one detects misuse, the other lowers the barrier to doing things correctly in the first place.

Analogy: Certificate Transparency is a public audit log every notary must publish; Let's Encrypt is making legitimate notarization free and automatic so nobody has an excuse to skip it.

Exam tip: Be ready to name Certificate Transparency specifically as the DigiNotar-motivated control, this pairing is a common exam link.

slides.title: Enforcing Strict Certificate Chain Validation
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: A common finding in security audits: applications with certificate validation disabled via flags such as verify=False or curl -k, which suppress TLS trust errors entirely.

Misconception: 'Disabling verification during dev and re-enabling before prod' rarely actually happens reliably, treat this as a control gap that must be actively audited for, not assumed fixed.

Analogy: Leaving your front door propped open 'just for a minute' during a move, then forgetting to close it once you're done.

Exam tip: A CN mismatch log entry should immediately trigger you to think: chain validation failure or active MITM, isolate and investigate.

Detection signal: a CN (common name) mismatch in logs is a textbook indicator of misconfiguration or interception
Full validation required: build and verify the chain to a trusted root, check validity window, confirm SAN matches
Reject, don't warn: clients should reject failing certificates rather than present a bypassable warning
Common failure: disabling verification (verify=False, curl -k) 'temporarily' during development, left in production

slides.title: Continuous Revocation Checking: CRLs and OCSP

quiz.question: A SOC detects repeated OCSP queries for a certificate that was already flagged as revoked. What does this most likely indicate?
options: A benign caching bug in the client's browser
An attacker attempting to reuse a compromised private key against clients that may not properly enforce revocation
The CA's OCSP responder is down
The certificate was renewed and the CA database has not updated yet
quiz.explanation: Option B is correct: repeated attempts to use a certificate already known to be revoked is a strong signal of an attacker trying to leverage a compromised key, hoping to reach a client configured to soft-fail on revocation checks. Options A, C, and D describe benign explanations that do not match the described pattern of repeated queries against a known-revoked certificate.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: RFC 6960 defines OCSP; RFC 6066 defines OCSP stapling.

Misconception: 'Revocation alone protects you.' It does nothing unless the checking client actually enforces it, a client configured to 'soft-fail' (proceed anyway if the OCSP responder is unreachable) defeats the purpose.

Analogy: A revoked certificate is like a cancelled credit card, the cancellation only works if the merchant's terminal actually checks the cancellation list instead of shrugging and approving the charge anyway.

Exam tip: Know the tradeoff: CRL = downloaded list, can be stale; OCSP = real-time, but adds a dependency on the CA's responder being reachable.
bullets: Certificate revocation: invalidating a certificate before its scheduled expiration, e.g. after key compromise
CRL (Certificate Revocation List): a downloadable list of revoked certificates, RFC 5280
OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol): real-time query 'is this cert still valid?', RFC 6960
OCSP stapling: server fetches and caches its own signed OCSP response, avoiding a client-to-CA round trip
Detection concern: repeated queries for a certificate already flagged revoked can indicate reuse of a compromised key

slides.title: Private Key Protection: HSMs and Lifecycle Management
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: FIPS 140-3 defines security levels for cryptographic modules, from Level 1 (software) to Level 4 (physical tamper response).

Misconception: 'A strong password protects the private key file well enough.' High-value keys (especially CA keys) require hardware-enforced protection, not just file-system permissions or passphrases.

Analogy: An HSM is a bank vault where the money (private key) never physically leaves, you can request a transaction be performed inside the vault, but you never get to hold the cash yourself.

Exam tip: Directly link this slide back to Heartbleed and DigiNotar: HSM-protected keys inside tamper-resistant hardware are far less likely to leak the way OpenSSL's in-memory key did.

HSM (Hardware Security Module): tamper-resistant hardware that generates/stores/uses keys without ever exposing raw key material
Root CA keys: should remain offline entirely, used only rarely to sign intermediate certificates
Standard: NIST SP 800-57 lifecycle guidance; FIPS 140-3 defines HSM security levels

slides.title: Defense in Depth for PKI
slides.speaker_notes:
Context (Exam Focus): Always identify that default configurations (accepting self-signed certificates, disabling verification for convenience) are themselves the vulnerability, not a secure baseline.

Misconception: Answering a PKI hardening question with just one control. Full credit typically requires naming controls across at least two of the three layers (technical/administrative/monitoring).

Analogy: Securing PKI is like securing a museum: locks on doors (technical), background checks on staff and audits (administrative), and cameras plus alarm monitoring (monitoring), removing any one layer doesn't make the others useless, but leaves a gap.

Exam tip: When asked to 'harden' a PKI deployment, structure your answer explicitly across all three layers for maximum credit.
bullets: Not a single control: a firewall filtering ports does nothing against a fraudulent cert over allowed port 443
Technical layer: strict chain validation, OCSP/CRL enforcement, HSM-protected keys
Administrative layer: CA audit requirements, key-rotation policy, certificate lifetime limits
Monitoring layer: Certificate Transparency log monitoring, SOC alerting on CN mismatches or anomalous OCSP patterns
Common trap: default configurations that accept self-signed certs or disable verification ARE the vulnerability

We generate a tiny key pair, encrypt and decrypt a number using modular exponentiation, and then simulate a signature check by comparing hashes before and after a message is tampered with.

code_block.content:
# Toy RSA demo with tiny primes (runs in Pyodide) -- illustrates the mechanism only.
# Real RSA uses primes hundreds of digits long; these are NOT secure.
p, q = 61, 53                  # tiny "primes" for readability
n = p * q                      # modulus
phi = (p - 1) * (q - 1)        # Euler's totient
e = 17                          # public exponent (must be coprime with phi)

def modinv(a, m):
    # extended Euclidean algorithm to find d = e^-1 mod phi
    g, x, _ = extended_gcd(a, m)
    return x % m

def extended_gcd(a, b):
    if a == 0:
        return b, 0, 1
    g, x1, y1 = extended_gcd(b % a, a)
    return g, y1 - (b // a) * x1, x1

d = modinv(e, phi)             # private exponent

m = 42                          # plaintext message (must be < n)
c = pow(m, e, n)                # ENCRYPT: c = m^e mod n
recovered = pow(c, d, n)        # DECRYPT: m = c^d mod n

print(f"public key (e,n) = ({e},{n})  private key (d,n) = ({d},{n})")
print(f"plaintext m={m} -> ciphertext c={c} -> decrypted={recovered}")
assert recovered == m, "decryption must recover the original plaintext"

# Simulated signature check via simple hash comparison
import hashlib
original = "contract v1: pay $500"
tampered = "contract v1: pay $500000"
print("original hash:", hashlib.sha256(original.encode()).hexdigest()[:16])
print("tampered hash:", hashlib.sha256(tampered.encode()).hexdigest()[:16])
print("Hashes match (signature would verify)?", hashlib.sha256(original.encode()).digest() == hashlib.sha256(tampered.encode()).digest())

slides.title: Synthesis: The Asymmetric Cryptography Kill Chain
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This 'kill chain' framing mirrors how the AP exam expects synthesis answers, trace an attack from initial trust establishment through to detection, naming which control breaks which link.

Misconception: Treating Heartbleed and DigiNotar as isolated trivia rather than two different attack points on the same underlying trust chain.

Analogy: A castle's defense isn't one wall, it's a sequence of gates (identity binding, handshake, key secrecy, revocation, transparency logs), and a real attacker only needs to find the one gate left open.

Exam tip: When asked for a comprehensive defense of a PKI deployment, walk through this exact chain and name a specific control at each stage, this earns maximum synthesis credit.
bullets: 1. Trust establishment: key pair generated, public key bound to identity via CA-signed X.509 certificate
2. Handshake: TLS validates the chain of trust, then ECDHE derives an ephemeral symmetric session key
3. Attacker goal, steal the private key: e.g. Heartbleed's memory-disclosure bug
4. Attacker goal, forge the trust itself: e.g. DigiNotar's CA compromise issuing fraudulent certificates
5. Defense chain: chain validation + revocation checking (OCSP/CRL) + HSM key protection + CT log monitoring breaks the attack at every stage

content_blocks: Pulling every section together: asymmetric cryptography's guarantees rest on a chain that can be attacked at multiple points. First, a key pair is generated and the public key is bound to a verified identity through a CA-signed X.509 certificate, this is the trust-establishment stage attackers target in a DigiNotar-style CA compromise. Second, the TLS handshake validates that chain of trust and derives an ephemeral symmetric session key via ECDHE, this stage depends on private keys staying secret, the exact guarantee Heartbleed broke through a memory-disclosure bug. Third, ongoing revocation checking (OCSP/CRL) and Certificate Transparency monitoring are what catch a compromise after the fact, when prevention alone has failed.

Every hardening control from Section IV maps to breaking this chain at a specific link: HSMs protect the private key from Heartbleed-style leaks; strict chain and CN validation stop a DigiNotar-style forged certificate from being silently accepted; OCSP/CRL enforcement invalidates a key even after compromise; Certificate Transparency detects fraudulent issuance even when a CA itself is compromised.

big_idea.text: A public/private key pair is a padlock that anyone can snap shut but only one specific key can open. You can mail that open padlock to the entire world and still be the only person alive who can unlock what it seals.
big_idea.closing: Hold onto this picture — we'll come back to it as the mechanics get more technical.
